fun_fact: The ringtail is California's state mammal, and its back feet can turn 180° so it can climb down cliffs headfirst.
where_to_find: Rocky canyons and cliffs near water; Pinnacles National Park and the canyons of Big Sur are good bets.
spotting_tip: Look for eyeshine on rocky canyon walls after dark, often near campgrounds and streams.

size: 2.5–3.5 ft long (75–105 cm), about 2 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Bobcats are named for their short, stubby 'bobbed' tail, only 4–7 inches long.
where_to_find: Point Reyes National Seashore's open grasslands, especially along Tomales Point and Abbotts Lagoon, are one of the best places to see bobcats hunting in daylight.
active_time: Dawn and dusk, sometimes midday in winter
spotting_tip: Scan open grassland edges slowly; bobcats often sit still watching gopher holes.
safety_note: Give it space and never feed it.

size: 3.5–4.5 ft long incl. tail (1.1–1.4 m), about 2 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Coyotes can sprint up to 40 mph and live in every part of California, including downtown Los Angeles.
where_to_find: Look in the grasslands of the Presidio and Golden Gate Park in San Francisco, or almost any open space at dawn and dusk.
spotting_tip: Listen for yipping at sunset, then scan open fields and trail edges.
safety_note: Never feed coyotes. Keep small pets close.

size: 2.5–3.5 ft long incl. tail (80–110 cm), about 14 in tall at shoulder
fun_fact: The gray fox is one of the only members of the dog family that can climb trees.
where_to_find: Try the oak woodlands of Mount Diablo State Park or Pinnacles National Park around dusk.
spotting_tip: Watch brushy edges of oak woodland at twilight; their gray coat with a rusty side is a giveaway.
safety_note: Never feed foxes.

size: 4–6 ft long (1.2–1.8 m), 2.5–3 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Most of California's 'black' bears are actually brown, cinnamon or blond.
where_to_find: Yosemite Valley and Sequoia National Park's Giant Forest have regular bear sightings; keep your distance and never feed them.
spotting_tip: Look in meadows and along streams, and stay at least 50 yards away.
safety_note: Never approach or feed a bear, and back away slowly if one comes toward you. Stay far from cubs.

size: 4–7 ft long (1.2–2.1 m), 3–3.5 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: Mule deer are named for their huge, mule-like ears, which swivel separately to track sounds.
where_to_find: Common in Yosemite Valley meadows and along the trails of Point Reyes and Mount Tamalpais.
spotting_tip: Look for them grazing at meadow edges; big ears turned toward you usually means one has spotted you first.
safety_note: Bucks can be aggressive in fall and does guard fawns in spring.

size: 6.5–8 ft long (2–2.5 m), 4–5 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: The Tule elk, found only in California, dropped to fewer than 30 animals in the 1870s and has recovered to over 5,000.
where_to_find: See Tule elk at Tomales Point in Point Reyes, or Roosevelt elk in the meadows of Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park.
spotting_tip: Scan open grassy hillsides; in fall, listen for males bugling.
safety_note: Bulls charge in fall (Aug–Oct) and cows guard calves in spring. Stay farther back in those seasons.

size: 4.5–6 ft long (1.4–1.8 m), about 3 ft tall at shoulder
fun_fact: A ram's curled horns can weigh 30 pounds, as much as all the bones in its body.
where_to_find: Scan the rocky slopes of Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, especially near Borrego Palm Canyon in the early morning.
spotting_tip: Glass rocky slopes near water sources with binoculars; their tan coat blends into the rocks.
safety_note: Protected species. Stay on trails and never approach.

fun_fact: Raccoons have super-sensitive front paws and often 'see' food by feeling it, especially when it's wet.
where_to_find: Common near creeks and campgrounds everywhere; try Lake Merritt in Oakland or Malibu Creek State Park after dark.
spotting_tip: Shine a flashlight along creeks and look for glowing eyes and hand-like tracks in the mud.
safety_note: Don't touch or feed. Raccoons bite and can carry disease.

fun_fact: A skunk can spray accurately up to about 10 feet, and usually stamps its feet as a warning first.
where_to_find: Watch for them at night in suburban parks and campgrounds, such as Bodega Bay or the East Bay Regional Parks.
spotting_tip: Look along trails and lawns after dark; keep your distance if one stamps its feet.
safety_note: Don't touch or feed, and back off if it stamps its feet or raises its tail.

fun_fact: The opossum is North America's only marsupial; babies ride in a pouch, then on their mother's back.
where_to_find: Look at night in backyards and city parks, like Golden Gate Park or Griffith Park.
spotting_tip: Check fences and trees in yards and parks with a flashlight; look for the pale face.
safety_note: Don't touch or feed.

fun_fact: Western gray squirrels bury thousands of acorns each fall and forget many of them, planting new oak trees.
where_to_find: Easy to spot in the oak and pine forests of Yosemite Valley and the Berkeley Hills.
spotting_tip: Look high in oaks and pines for a silver-gray squirrel with a big fluffy tail.

fun_fact: These squirrels chew shed rattlesnake skins and lick the scent onto their fur to disguise their smell.
where_to_find: Everywhere in open grassy areas; Crissy Field in San Francisco and Shoreline Park in Mountain View are full of them.
spotting_tip: Look for burrow holes in open grass and wait; they pop up to watch for danger.

fun_fact: Desert cottontails rarely drink; they get most of their water from the plants they eat.
where_to_find: Look along trail edges at dawn in Joshua Tree National Park or the Santa Monica Mountains.
spotting_tip: Walk slowly along trail edges; they freeze before they run, giving you a moment for a photo.

size: 1.5–2 ft long (47–63 cm), ears up to 7 in
fun_fact: A jackrabbit's giant ears work like radiators, releasing body heat to keep it cool in the desert.
where_to_find: Common in open fields at dusk; try the Carrizo Plain, Antelope Valley or the edges of Joshua Tree.
spotting_tip: Look in open fields; their long black-tipped ears stick up above the grass.

fun_fact: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch.
where_to_find: Elkhorn Slough near Moss Landing and the Monterey Bay Coastal Trail are the best places to watch sea otters up close.
active_time: Daytime, most active morning and late afternoon
spotting_tip: Look for floating 'logs' in kelp beds that turn out to be otters lying on their backs.
safety_note: If an otter looks at you or dives, you're too close. Disturbing otters is illegal.

fun_fact: River otters can hold their breath for up to 8 minutes and close their ears and nostrils underwater.
where_to_find: Look at Lake Merritt's channel, the Sacramento River Delta, or Rodeo Lagoon in the Marin Headlands.
spotting_tip: Look for V-shaped ripples in calm water and slides on muddy banks.
safety_note: Otters bite. Watch from a distance.

size: 6–8 ft long males, 5–6 ft females (1.5–2.4 m)
fun_fact: Sea lions can 'walk' on land by rotating their back flippers forward, which true seals can't do.
where_to_find: Pier 39 in San Francisco and La Jolla Cove in San Diego have big, noisy crowds of sea lions year-round.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud barking near piers and buoys.
safety_note: Sea lions bite. Disturbing marine mammals is illegal under federal law.

fun_fact: Each harbor seal has a unique spot pattern, like a fingerprint.
where_to_find: Point Lobos, Children's Pool in La Jolla, and Jenner at the mouth of the Russian River are reliable spots.
active_time: Low tide, any time of day
spotting_tip: Look for 'bananas' resting on rocks and sand at low tide, and stay quiet so they don't flush.
safety_note: If a seal lifts its head or moves away, you're too close. Never approach pups on the beach.

size: Males up to 13 ft (4 m), females up to 10 ft (3 m)
weight: Males up to 5,000 lb (2,300 kg), females 900–1,800 lb
fun_fact: Elephant seals can dive more than a mile deep and stay underwater for up to 2 hours.
where_to_find: Visit the Piedras Blancas viewpoint near San Simeon or Año Nuevo State Park, especially in winter.
active_time: Daytime, biggest crowds December to March
spotting_tip: Visit viewpoints in winter to see huge males fighting and new pups.
safety_note: Males weigh up to 2 tons and charge fast. View only from official viewing areas.

fun_fact: Male humpbacks sing complex songs that can last 20 minutes and be heard many miles away.
where_to_find: Take a whale-watching trip out of Monterey Bay, or scan from Point Reyes Lighthouse in spring and summer.
spotting_tip: Look for spouts and tail flukes on the horizon on calm days.
safety_note: Photograph from shore or a licensed whale-watching boat only. Approaching whales is illegal.

fun_fact: Marmots can hibernate for up to 8 months a year in the high Sierra.
where_to_find: Look on sunny granite boulders at Tioga Pass and Tuolumne Meadows in Yosemite during summer.
spotting_tip: Look for them sunbathing on big granite boulders near meadows.

size: 6–8 in long (15–20 cm), no visible tail
fun_fact: Pikas don't hibernate; all summer they cut and dry 'haypiles' of plants to eat under the winter snow.
where_to_find: Listen for their squeaks in high rock piles around Tioga Pass or Mono Pass in the Sierra, above 8,000 feet.
spotting_tip: Stop at high-elevation rock piles and listen for a sharp 'eep!', then look for a small round gray body.

fun_fact: The California Quail is the state bird; its forward-curling head plume is made of six feathers.
where_to_find: Common in brushy parks and chaparral; try Point Reyes, Mount Diablo, or the Santa Monica Mountains.
spotting_tip: Listen for the 'chi-CAH-go' call and look under shrubs for a covey on the ground.

fun_fact: The fierce scream you hear for eagles in movies is almost always a red-tailed hawk.
where_to_find: Look on light poles and fence posts along almost any highway, or soaring over the Marin Headlands.
spotting_tip: Check light poles and fence posts along roads; look for the rusty red tail.

fun_fact: Steller's jays often imitate the red-shouldered hawk's call so well that it fools other birds.
where_to_find: Common in leafy neighborhoods and creekside parks, like Stanford's campus or the Los Angeles River trails.
spotting_tip: Listen for a loud repeated 'kee-ah' near creeks and wooded neighborhoods.

size: 9–12 in long (22–31 cm), about 2 ft wingspan
fun_fact: The kestrel is North America's smallest falcon and can hover in place while hunting.
where_to_find: Look on power lines over open fields, like the Carrizo Plain or the farmland around Davis.
spotting_tip: Look for a small falcon on power lines that bobs its tail or hovers over fields.

fun_fact: Bald eagle nests can grow to 10 feet wide and weigh over a ton after years of additions.
where_to_find: Big Bear Lake and Lake Cachuma host wintering bald eagles, and Shasta Lake has them year-round.
spotting_tip: Scan tall dead trees near lakeshores and look for the white head.
safety_note: Protected by federal law. Never approach a nest.

fun_fact: Golden eagles can dive at more than 150 mph when chasing prey.
where_to_find: Scan the skies over the Altamont Pass hills, Mount Diablo, or the Carrizo Plain.
spotting_tip: Look for a huge dark bird soaring in slow circles over open hills.
safety_note: Protected by federal law. Never approach a nest.

fun_fact: Ospreys plunge feet-first into water and turn the fish head-forward to carry it in flight.
where_to_find: Watch for nesting ospreys at Richmond's Marina Bay, Lake Tahoe, or Morro Bay.
spotting_tip: Look for big stick nests on poles and platforms near water, and watch for feet-first dives.
safety_note: Never approach a nest.

size: 25–32 in long (64–81 cm), about 6 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Turkey vultures can smell carrion from more than a mile away, rare for a bird.
where_to_find: Seen soaring over almost any hillside; Hawk Hill in the Marin Headlands has hundreds in fall.
spotting_tip: Look for big dark birds rocking side to side in a V-shape as they soar.

size: 3.5–4.5 ft long (1.1–1.4 m), up to 9.5 ft wingspan
fun_fact: With a wingspan up to 9.5 feet, the condor is North America's largest flying land bird; in 1987 only 27 were left.
where_to_find: Pinnacles National Park and the Big Sur coast are the best places to see condors soaring.
active_time: Late morning to afternoon, when the air warms
spotting_tip: Look for very big birds with white patches under the wings and numbered wing tags.
safety_note: Critically endangered. Never approach, feed or disturb one.

fun_fact: Great horned owls are one of the few animals that regularly hunt skunks.
where_to_find: Listen for hooting at dusk in Griffith Park, Golden Gate Park, or oak woodlands across the state.
spotting_tip: Listen for deep 'hoo-hoo-HOO-hoo-hoo' hooting at dusk, then look for the silhouette on a high branch.
safety_note: Don't approach nests or use flash on owls.

fun_fact: Barn owls can catch mice in total darkness using hearing alone.
where_to_find: Look at dusk over farm fields and marshes, like the Palo Alto Baylands or the Sacramento Valley.
spotting_tip: Watch farm fields and marshes at dusk for a pale ghostly bird gliding low.
safety_note: Don't approach nests or use flash on owls.

fun_fact: During courtship dives, male Anna's hummingbirds hit about 60 mph and make a chirp with their tail feathers.
where_to_find: Found year-round in gardens and parks; the San Francisco Botanical Garden is full of them.
spotting_tip: Watch flowering bushes and feeders; males flash a pink-red throat in the sun.

fun_fact: Acorn woodpeckers store acorns in 'granary trees' that can hold up to 50,000 acorns, each in its own hole.
where_to_find: Look for their granary trees in oak woodlands at Pinnacles, Mount Diablo, or Hastings Reserve.
spotting_tip: Look for trees and poles full of holes stuffed with acorns, then wait for the noisy 'ja-cob' calls.

fun_fact: Unlike most woodpeckers, flickers mostly feed on the ground, licking up ants with a long, sticky tongue.
where_to_find: Watch lawns and open woods in winter, like Golden Gate Park or Yosemite Valley.
spotting_tip: Look on lawns for a brown bird with a white rump that flashes when it flies.

fun_fact: Scrub-jays hide thousands of food items and remember where, and even which hiding spots others watched.
where_to_find: Common in suburban yards and oak parks; Tilden Park in Berkeley is a sure bet.
spotting_tip: Easy to find in yards and parks; listen for its harsh scratchy call.

fun_fact: Steller's jays are excellent mimics and can imitate hawks, squirrels, cats and even dogs.
where_to_find: Easy to find around picnic areas in Yosemite, Lake Tahoe, and the redwood parks.
spotting_tip: Look around picnic tables in mountain forests; they come to you.

fun_fact: Crows can recognize individual human faces and remember people who treated them badly for years.
where_to_find: Common in cities and farm towns; try Sacramento's parks or the Los Angeles suburbs.
spotting_tip: Easy in towns; look for flocks gathering at sunset to roost.

size: 22–27 in long (56–69 cm), about 4 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Ravens are bigger than crows, have wedge-shaped tails, and do barrel rolls and somersaults in flight.
where_to_find: Look along the Big Sur coast, at Joshua Tree, or at Yosemite viewpoints.
spotting_tip: Look for a wedge-shaped tail and listen for a deep croak instead of a 'caw'.

fun_fact: Black phoebes build cup-shaped nests out of mud, often under bridges and eaves.
where_to_find: Almost always near water; look along creeks and ponds like the Palo Alto Baylands or the LA River.
spotting_tip: Look near water for a small black-and-white bird flicking its tail on a low perch.

fun_fact: Young western bluebirds often stay to help their parents raise the next brood.
where_to_find: Look in open oak woodlands and golf courses, like Mount Diablo or Henry Coe State Park.
spotting_tip: Scan fences and low branches in open woodland for a flash of blue.

fun_fact: Robins find earthworms mostly by sight, tilting their heads to look closely at the ground.
where_to_find: Common on lawns in spring and summer, and in big berry-eating flocks in winter parks.
spotting_tip: Look on damp lawns for a bird hopping and tilting its head to find worms.

fun_fact: A male mockingbird can learn up to 200 different songs, including car alarms.
where_to_find: Sings from rooftops and treetops in towns, especially in Southern California neighborhoods.
active_time: Daytime, and singing on spring nights
spotting_tip: Listen for a bird singing many different songs in a row from a high perch.

fun_fact: California towhees often fight their own reflections in car mirrors and windows.
where_to_find: Look on the ground under shrubs in gardens and chaparral parks, like Tilden or Griffith Park.
spotting_tip: Look for a plain brown bird scratching in leaves under bushes.

fun_fact: White-crowned sparrows from different areas sing in local 'dialects', like regional accents.
where_to_find: Common in winter in parks and gardens; the coastal scrub of the Presidio has them year-round.
spotting_tip: Look for a striped black-and-white head on sparrows feeding on the ground.

fun_fact: A male house finch's red color comes from pigments in its food; the redder he is, the better he ate.
where_to_find: Common at backyard feeders and in city parks everywhere in California.
spotting_tip: Easy at feeders and on rooftops; males have a red head and chest.

fun_fact: Male red-winged blackbirds puff out their red shoulder patches to defend territory and attract mates.
where_to_find: Look in cattail marshes, like Lake Merced in San Francisco or the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge.
spotting_tip: Listen for 'conk-la-ree!' from cattails and look for red shoulder patches.

fun_fact: The yellow-billed magpie lives nowhere in the world except California's Central Valley and coastal valleys.
where_to_find: Look in the Central Valley, around UC Davis's campus or Cosumnes River Preserve.
spotting_tip: Look in tall trees around farms and parks in the Central Valley for a black-and-white bird with a long tail.

size: 3.2–4.5 ft tall (1–1.4 m), about 6 ft wingspan
fun_fact: Despite standing over 4 feet tall, a great blue heron weighs only about 5 pounds thanks to hollow bones.
where_to_find: Watch marshes and lakeshores like Bolsa Chica Ecological Reserve, Elkhorn Slough, or Lake Merritt.
spotting_tip: Look for a tall gray bird standing motionless in shallow water.

fun_fact: Great egrets were nearly wiped out for their feathers in the 1800s, which led to the founding of the Audubon Society.
where_to_find: Common in wetlands; Bolsa Chica, the Palo Alto Baylands, and Audubon Canyon Ranch in Marin have many.
spotting_tip: Look for a tall all-white bird with a yellow bill wading in marshes.

fun_fact: Brown pelicans plunge-dive from up to 60 feet and scoop up to 3 gallons of water in their pouch.
where_to_find: Watch them dive along the coast at La Jolla Cove, Monterey's Fisherman's Wharf, or Santa Cruz Wharf.
spotting_tip: Watch the ocean for lines of pelicans gliding low or splashing headfirst into the water.

fun_fact: Only female mallards make the classic loud 'quack'; males make a quieter, raspy sound.
where_to_find: Found on nearly any pond or lake, like Lake Merritt or Echo Park Lake in Los Angeles.
spotting_tip: Easy on almost any pond; males have a shiny green head.

fun_fact: Canada geese fly in a V so each bird gets a lift from the air swirling off the wingtips of the one ahead.
where_to_find: Common in city parks and golf courses, like Shoreline Lake in Mountain View.
spotting_tip: Look on lawns near lakes and golf courses.

fun_fact: Western gulls take four years to get their adult white and dark-gray feathers.
where_to_find: Common on beaches and piers along the whole coast, especially Santa Monica Pier and Pier 39.
spotting_tip: Easy on beaches and piers; look for the dark-gray back and pink legs.

fun_fact: Despite the name, Black Oystercatchers mostly eat mussels and limpets, prying them open with a chisel-like red bill.
where_to_find: Rocky shores at Point Pinos, Point Lobos, Fitzgerald Marine Reserve, Bodega Head and Point Reyes.
spotting_tip: Listen for loud whistles and scan wave-washed rocks for a black bird with a bright red bill.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

size: 20–24 in long (50–62 cm), including a long tail
fun_fact: Roadrunners can run about 20 mph and are fast enough to catch and eat rattlesnakes.
where_to_find: Look in desert scrub at Anza-Borrego, Joshua Tree, or the edges of Palm Springs.
spotting_tip: Watch roadsides and open desert for a long-tailed bird running fast.

fun_fact: A protein in fence lizard blood kills the Lyme disease bacteria in ticks that feed on them.
where_to_find: Easy to spot doing push-ups on sunny rocks and fences in almost any park, like Mount Diablo.
spotting_tip: Look on sunny rocks, logs and fences for lizards doing push-ups.

fun_fact: Alligator lizards can drop their tails to escape predators, and the tail keeps wriggling as a distraction.
where_to_find: Look under logs and in leaf litter in gardens and oak woodlands, like Tilden Park.
spotting_tip: Look carefully under boards and in leaf litter, then put everything back.

fun_fact: Male side-blotched lizards come in three throat colors that compete like rock, paper, scissors.
where_to_find: Common on sunny rocks in Joshua Tree, Anza-Borrego, and the Inland Empire foothills.
spotting_tip: Look on sunny rocks for a small lizard with a dark spot behind each front leg.

fun_fact: Young western skinks have bright blue tails that attract predators away from their bodies.
where_to_find: Look under rocks and logs in grassy oak woodlands, like Henry Coe or Pinnacles.
spotting_tip: Look for a flash of bright blue tail when you turn over rocks or logs.

fun_fact: When threatened, horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes up to 3 feet.
where_to_find: Look on sandy open ground in the Pinnacles, the Carrizo Plain, or coastal sage scrub in San Diego County.
active_time: Warm mornings in spring and summer
spotting_tip: Watch sandy open ground closely; they rely on camouflage and stay very still.
safety_note: Protected species. Don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Desert iguanas stay active in heat up to 115°F, hotter than almost any other lizard can stand.
where_to_find: Watch creosote bush flats on hot days in Joshua Tree, Anza-Borrego, or the Mojave Preserve.
spotting_tip: Look on sand near creosote bushes when it's too hot for most other lizards.

fun_fact: Gopher snakes hiss loudly and shake their tails to imitate rattlesnakes, but they're harmless.
where_to_find: Look on warm trails in grasslands and chaparral, like Mount Diablo or the Santa Monica Mountains.
active_time: Daytime in spring, evening in summer
spotting_tip: Watch warm trails and grassy edges, and enjoy them from a distance.

fun_fact: Kingsnakes are immune to rattlesnake venom and sometimes eat rattlesnakes.
where_to_find: Look in chaparral and oak woodland in the early morning, like Pinnacles or the Santa Monica Mountains.
spotting_tip: Look near rocks and logs in chaparral for black-and-white or brown-and-cream bands.

fun_fact: The San Francisco garter snake, a red, black and turquoise form, is often called America's most beautiful snake.
where_to_find: Look near ponds and marshes; the San Francisco garter snake lives around Mori Point in Pacifica.
spotting_tip: Look along pond and stream edges on sunny days.

fun_fact: A rattlesnake adds a new rattle segment each time it sheds, so counting segments doesn't tell its age.
where_to_find: Found on sunny trails in Mount Diablo, Pinnacles, and the Sierra foothills; watch from a safe distance.
active_time: Daytime in spring and fall, evening in summer
spotting_tip: Watch the trail ahead and listen for the rattle; never approach.
safety_note: Never touch or try to move a rattlesnake. Use zoom and step back the way you came.

fun_fact: The western pond turtle is the only native freshwater turtle in most of California.
where_to_find: Look for them basking on logs in quiet ponds, like those at Point Reyes National Seashore or the sloughs of the Sacramento River Delta.
spotting_tip: Scan logs and rocks in ponds with binoculars before they slide into the water.
safety_note: Declining species. Don't pick it up.

size: Shell 9–15 in long (23–38 cm), 4–6 in tall
fun_fact: Desert tortoises can live 50–80 years and spend about 95% of their lives in underground burrows.
where_to_find: Look in spring at the Desert Tortoise Research Natural Area near California City, or the Mojave National Preserve.
spotting_tip: Look near burrows and wildflower patches in spring; never pick one up.
safety_note: Threatened species. It's illegal to touch, pick up or move one.

fun_fact: Treefrogs can change color between green and brown in minutes to match their surroundings.
where_to_find: Listen for 'ribbit' choruses at night near any pond or creek in winter and spring, like Point Reyes.
spotting_tip: Follow the 'ribbit' chorus with a flashlight to pond edges.

fun_fact: California newts carry tetrodotoxin, the same powerful poison found in pufferfish.
where_to_find: Look on wet trails after winter rains in the Santa Monica Mountains or the Santa Cruz Mountains.
active_time: Rainy days in winter and spring
spotting_tip: Walk wet trails after rain and look on the ground; watch your step.
safety_note: Its skin is toxic. Don't handle it, and wash your hands if you do.

fun_fact: Ensatinas have no lungs and breathe entirely through their moist skin.
where_to_find: Look under logs on damp days in redwood forests like Muir Woods or Big Basin.
spotting_tip: Gently lift logs in moist forest, look, and put them back.

fun_fact: Bullfrogs aren't native to California and will eat almost anything that fits in their mouths, including snakes and birds.
where_to_find: Listen for their deep calls at ponds and reservoirs, like Lake Merced or any golf course pond.
spotting_tip: Follow the deep 'jug-o-rum' calls and look for eyes at the water's edge.

fun_fact: Monarchs from the West spend winter in clusters of thousands at groves along the California coast.
where_to_find: Visit Pacific Grove's Monarch Grove Sanctuary or Natural Bridges State Beach in Santa Cruz from November to February.
spotting_tip: Look up into eucalyptus and cypress trees for brown clusters that turn orange when they open their wings.

fun_fact: Groups of tiger swallowtails gather at puddles to sip water and minerals, which is called 'puddling'.
where_to_find: Common in spring and summer in gardens and along creeks, like Golden Gate Park or Yosemite Valley.
spotting_tip: Watch flowers and wet mud along creeks.

fun_fact: Pipevine swallowtails are toxic to birds because their caterpillars eat poisonous pipevine plants.
where_to_find: Look along creeks with pipevine plants in spring, like the American River Parkway.
spotting_tip: Look for dark butterflies with shiny blue hindwings near pipevine plants by creeks.

fun_fact: Mourning cloaks can live 10–11 months, one of the longest lifespans of any butterfly.
where_to_find: One of the first butterflies of spring; look along willow-lined creeks, like the Sierra foothills.
spotting_tip: Look for dark wings with a cream border basking on sunny paths.

fun_fact: Painted ladies migrate in huge swarms; in 2019 a swarm over Southern California was so big it showed up on weather radar.
where_to_find: Very common in spring, especially in years when swarms migrate north through Southern California.
spotting_tip: Watch fields of wildflowers, especially during migration years.

fun_fact: A honey bee does a 'waggle dance' to tell its hive the direction and distance to flowers.
where_to_find: Found on flowers everywhere; the UC Davis Bee Haven garden is a great place to watch them.
spotting_tip: Watch any patch of flowers.
safety_note: Bees sting. Don't disturb a hive, and keep away if you're allergic.

fun_fact: Millions of convergent lady beetles gather in mountain canyons to spend winter in huge clumps.
where_to_find: Huge winter clusters gather in canyons like Redwood Regional Park and the Sierra foothills.
spotting_tip: Look for orange clumps on logs and shrubs in shady canyons in winter.

size: 2–2.5 in long (5–6 cm), wingspan about 3.5 in
fun_fact: Male flame skimmers are bright orange-red from head to tail, even their wing veins.
where_to_find: Look around ponds and slow streams in summer, like the LA Arboretum or Lake Elizabeth in Fremont.
spotting_tip: Look for a bright orange dragonfly perched on sticks at the edge of a pond.

fun_fact: A mantis can turn its head about 180 degrees to look over its shoulder.
where_to_find: Look in late summer on shrubs and grasses in gardens and parks, especially in Southern California.
spotting_tip: Search shrubs and tall grass slowly; mantises stay very still.

size: Female body about 0.5 in (13 mm), male much smaller
fun_fact: Black widow silk is one of the strongest spider silks, and was once used for crosshairs in gun sights.
where_to_find: Look in dark corners of woodpiles and sheds at night; look, but never touch.
spotting_tip: Look with a flashlight for a shiny black spider with a red hourglass in its messy web; don't touch.
safety_note: Venomous. Look but never touch, and check gloves and shoes in garages and woodpiles.

fun_fact: Banana slugs are among the largest land slugs in the world, and California has several kinds; any of them counts here.
where_to_find: Look on the forest floor after rain at Muir Woods, Big Basin, or UC Santa Cruz.
spotting_tip: Look on the forest floor and on logs after rain, especially in redwoods.

fun_fact: Ochre sea stars eat mussels by pushing their stomach out of their mouth and into the shell.
where_to_find: Visit the tide pools at Fitzgerald Marine Reserve, Point Lobos, or Cabrillo National Monument at low tide.
spotting_tip: Go at a low tide (check a tide chart) and look on rocks and in crevices.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Bat stars come in almost every color, from orange and red to purple, green and brown.
where_to_find: Look in tide pools and shallow water at Point Lobos or Monterey's Asilomar State Beach.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools and shallow rocky water at low tide.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Purple urchins can chew holes into solid rock with their five teeth to make a home.
where_to_find: Look in rocky tide pools at Fitzgerald Marine Reserve or Pescadero State Beach.
spotting_tip: Look in rocky tide pools for purple spiky balls tucked into holes.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

size: Up to 7 in tall and 10 in across (18 x 25 cm)
fun_fact: Its green color comes from tiny algae living inside its tissues, which make food from sunlight.
where_to_find: Look in tide pools at Asilomar, Pescadero, or Cabrillo National Monument.
spotting_tip: Look in tide pools for bright green 'flowers' that close when touched.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Lined shore crabs can hold water in their gill chambers and spend hours out of the ocean.
where_to_find: Scuttle-watch on rocks at the edge of the water at nearly any rocky beach, like La Jolla Cove.
spotting_tip: Sit still near rocks at the water's edge and wait for them to come out.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Hermit crabs don't grow their own shell: they move into empty snail shells, often Black Turban Snail shells, and trade up as they grow.
where_to_find: Almost any rocky tide pool at low tide, e.g. Fitzgerald Marine Reserve, Point Pinos, Crystal Cove and Cabrillo National Monument.
spotting_tip: Sit still beside a shallow pool for a minute; the 'snails' that start walking are hermit crabs. Look for blue bands on the legs.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Black Turban Snails can live 20–30 years, and worn shells show a pearly purple tip.
where_to_find: Upper and middle tide pools along the whole coast; huge numbers at Point Pinos, Asilomar and Crystal Cove.
spotting_tip: Look on rocks and in shallow pools near the top of the tide zone, where they gather in groups.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: California mussels anchor themselves with threads so strong that scientists study them to make waterproof glues.
where_to_find: Wave-washed rocks on the open coast, e.g. Duxbury Reef, Point Pinos, Leo Carrillo and Cabrillo National Monument.
spotting_tip: Look for dense blue-black beds on rocks facing the waves, and photograph from a safe spot above the surf.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

size: Up to 4 in long incl. stalk (10 cm)
fun_fact: Unlike most barnacles, gooseneck barnacles sit on a fleshy stalk and catch food from crashing waves with feathery legs.
where_to_find: Wave-pounded rocks among the mussel beds at Point Pinos, Fitzgerald Marine Reserve, Duxbury Reef and Leo Carrillo.
spotting_tip: Check gaps in mussel beds on rocks facing the surf for tight clusters of leathery 'necks' tipped with white plates.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Each owl limpet farms its own patch of algae and shoves other snails off it; the scar inside its shell looks like an owl.
where_to_find: High rocks at Cabrillo National Monument, Crystal Cove, Leo Carrillo and Point Lobos.
spotting_tip: Scan sunny rocks in the upper tide zone for large oval brown shells with a bare, grazed patch around them.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

weight: Usually 1–2 lb (0.5–1 kg), rarely much more
fun_fact: When bothered, a sea hare squirts a harmless cloud of purple ink to confuse predators.
where_to_find: Calm tide pools and eelgrass in Southern and Central California, e.g. Crystal Cove, Cabrillo National Monument and Point Dume.
spotting_tip: Look for a big reddish-brown blob with two 'rabbit ear' tentacles in shallow pools.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Hopkins' Rose gets its hot-pink color from the pink animals it eats; some years thousands appear in Monterey tide pools.
where_to_find: Rocky tide pools in Central California, especially Point Pinos, Asilomar and Fitzgerald Marine Reserve.
active_time: Very low tides, spring and fall
spotting_tip: Look under ledges in the lowest pools for tiny bright-pink frilly blobs; move slowly and look closely.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Tidepool sculpins have a homing sense: moved to a different pool, many find their way back to their own.
where_to_find: Shallow rocky tide pools from Monterey north, e.g. Point Pinos, Fitzgerald Marine Reserve and Duxbury Reef.
spotting_tip: Watch the bottom of a calm pool for a small mottled fish that darts and freezes; shade the water with your body to cut glare.
safety_note: Watch the waves and never turn your back on the ocean. Look, don't pick it up.

fun_fact: Each By-the-wind Sailor has a small stiff sail, and after spring winds millions can wash up on one beach.
where_to_find: Sandy beaches along the whole coast after onshore spring winds, e.g. Ocean Beach (San Francisco), Santa Cruz and Pismo.
spotting_tip: Walk the high-tide line on sandy beaches for small blue disks with a clear sail on top.
safety_note: It has mild stinging cells. Avoid touching it, then your eyes.

fun_fact: The garibaldi is California's official state marine fish, and males make clicking sounds to guard their nests.
where_to_find: Snorkel at La Jolla Cove or Avalon's Casino Point Dive Park on Catalina Island.
spotting_tip: Snorkel in rocky kelp areas and look for a bright orange fish guarding its spot.
safety_note: Protected state fish. Photograph from shore, or snorkel only in calm water with a buddy.
